question: A patient reports that individual swellings on her skin each persist for approximately 36 hours, are painful rather than purely itchy, and leave a brownish discolouration when they fade. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the appropriate next step?

answers.text: Urticarial vasculitis; perform a skin biopsy to look for leucocytoclastic vasculitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The triad of lesions persisting >24 hours, pain or burning rather than pure itch, and resolution with bruising or post-inflammatory pigmentation is characteristic of urticarial vasculitis — a small-vessel vasculitis. A skin biopsy confirming leucocytoclastic vasculitis establishes the diagnosis and directs a different management approach.

In urticaria, individual wheals last less than 24 hours, are itchy (not primarily painful), and resolve without leaving any mark. Lesions persisting beyond 24 hours with pain and residual pigmentation suggest urticarial vasculitis, which requires biopsy confirmation.

answers.text: Chronic spontaneous urticaria; order thyroid function tests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic spontaneous urticaria shares the fundamental wheal behaviour of all urticaria — each lesion is transient (<24 hours) and resolves without a mark. Persistent, painful lesions that leave pigmentation point to urticarial vasculitis, not chronic urticaria.

answers.text: Allergic contact dermatitis; identify and remove the allergen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Contact dermatitis presents with eczematous changes (erythema, vesicles, scaling) at the site of allergen exposure, not with recurrent deep swellings. The pattern of persistent painful lesions with residual pigmentation points to urticarial vasculitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three features that separate urticarial vasculitis from ordinary urticaria: lesions lasting >24 hours, painful or burning rather than itchy, and resolution with bruising or pigmentation. Any of these should prompt a skin biopsy.
Well recognised. These three red-flag features — persistence >24 hours, pain instead of itch, and residual pigmentation — should always prompt suspicion of urticarial vasculitis and a skin biopsy.
